text:
☕ Every week I look at what is winning on Chinese marketing platforms, and this week one story beat everything else, including campaigns with real budgets. A pancake shop next to a Luckin Coffee outlet posted a seven second video. Luckin answered with a short film. Chinese netizens are calling it the best PR move of the year. Here is what happened, and what it means for any foreign brand trying to build a following in China.

![Luckin Coffee neighbor pancake shop owner holding coffee and flatbread in front of the two stores](https://marketingtochina.com/wp-content/uploads/luckin-coffee-pancake-shop-neighbor-ad.png)

## A seven second video from a small town in Shandong

The story starts in Puji Town, a small town in the Zhangqiu district of Jinan, Shandong province. A woman runs a local 火烧 (huoshao) and 油饼 shop, selling grilled flatbread and fried dough, the kind of stall you find on almost every Chinese street. When a Luckin Coffee outlet opened right next to her shop, she noticed something simple. More people were walking past. More people were stopping. She filmed a short video on Douyin and said, in her own words, that her turnover went up as soon as Luckin opened. The video is not polished. It is a woman in front of her shop, talking about her sales. It got around 150,000 likes.

That kind of organic praise is rare for any brand, and Luckin’s team noticed it. Instead of ignoring the video or simply reposting it, Luckin sent a crew to Puji Town and made an actual short film about it.

## Luckin’s reply: a proper ad, not a repost

The result was a short branded film with a title that translates roughly as “Luckin’s Big Flatbread” (瑞幸大烧饼). It was produced with agency MIND WAY (传意互动), based in Beijing, with a Luckin vice president known online as 三月 personally involved in the project. The film is built around one line, spoken by the brand back to the shop owner: 其实和你们做邻居是我们的幸运, “actually, being your neighbor is our luck.”

What makes the film work is what it does not do. It does not turn the pancake shop into a Luckin prop. The camera also visits the lamb skewer stall, the hot and sour soup stand, and the fried chicken shop nearby, treating them all as part of the same street rather than as competitors for attention. Luckin positions its coffee as one more stall on a street that was already full of life before it arrived, not as the reason the street matters. That framing, a global chain thanking the small, older businesses around it instead of talking about itself, is unusual enough in Chinese advertising that it became the whole story.

## Why this became the case study everyone is sharing

This case was picked up by Digitaling (数英网), one of the main trade sites Chinese marketers use to track what is actually working, under the title “瑞幸给隔壁烧饼店拍了支广告，片名叫《瑞幸大烧饼》”. On Xiaohongshu, the response film passed 100,000 likes. Comments compared the production quality to a state television public service ad, and one widely liked comment simply thanked the shop owner for the “luck and inspiration” she gave the brand by accident. Chinese netizens gave it a label that is hard to earn and impossible to buy: 年度封神公关, “the PR of the year.”

Two things stand out for anyone studying Chinese marketing right now. First, Luckin did not build a campaign around a celebrity or a big product launch. It built one around a real person who had nothing to gain from flattering the brand, which is exactly why it was believed. Second, the response respected the local business instead of using it. There was no coupon code stapled to the shop owner’s story, no “collab menu,” just recognition. If you want to see how this kind of thinking shows up across other recent Chinese campaigns, I broke down the sharpest examples in our Top 50 China Ad Campaigns of H1 2026, and if you are weighing whether a formal tie-up with a local partner makes sense for your brand, our guide to co-branding in China covers the mechanics.

## Philip Chen’s take: why self-deprecation and small collabs work in China

I have watched a lot of “big brand meets small business” stories in China over the years, and the ones that work share one trait. The big brand goes first, and it goes small. Luckin did not ask the pancake shop for anything. It thanked her, on camera, before she asked for anything either. In a market where consumers are tired of being sold to, a brand that visibly gives credit away, instead of taking it, earns more trust in three minutes than most product ads earn in three months.

There is also a cultural reason self-deprecation travels so well here. Chinese social media users are quick to punish a brand that takes itself too seriously, and just as quick to reward one that can laugh at its own size and reach. A coffee chain with thousands of stores admitting that a flatbread stall helped its business, instead of the other way around, flips the expected power relationship. That reversal is what got people talking, not the coffee.

For a foreign brand, the instinct is often to copy the format: find a small local shop, film something warm, add a logo. That usually looks forced, because the audience can tell when gratitude is manufactured for content rather than felt. The part worth copying is not the video. It is the posture. Before you plan your next China campaign, ask a simpler question first: who around your business, a supplier, a local partner, a store neighbor, has quietly helped you without asking for credit? Start there, with something true and small, before you start with something big and produced. A foreign brand does not need Luckin’s production budget to borrow Luckin’s instinct. It needs to notice the people next door and say so, in public, before anyone asks it to.

One practical starting point: if your brand works with local distributors, retail partners, or even a single landlord relationship in a Chinese city, that relationship is content. Most foreign brands never think to film it. This case is a reminder that Chinese audiences reward brands that treat the people around them as part of the story, not just the supply chain behind it. China’s coffee category in particular has become a useful mirror for this shift, which I looked at in more detail in why China’s coffee industry is on fire.

*Source (Chinese): 数英网 (Digitaling), “瑞幸给隔壁烧饼店拍了支广告，片名叫《瑞幸大烧饼》,” July 2026. The article reports the original Douyin video’s 150,000 likes, the Xiaohongshu response film’s 100,000-plus likes, agency MIND WAY (传意互动), and the netizen label “年度封神公关” (PR of the year).*

**About the author.** Philip Chen is CEO of GMA (Gentlemen Marketing Agency), a digital marketing agency focused on the Chinese market. GMA has helped more than 1,000 brands grow in China across Baidu, WeChat, Douyin, Xiaohongshu and cross border e-commerce. Connect with Philip on LinkedIn.
title: Luckin Coffee's Viral Pancake Shop Ad: What Hyperlocal Humor Teaches Foreign Brands in China
